title: The First Number You Hear Bends Your Guess
hook_line: The first number you see quietly steers your guess.
full_voiceover: The first number you see quietly steers your guess. Psychologists call it anchoring. In a classic study, people spun a wheel of numbers before answering. They estimated the share of African countries in the United Nations. The wheel's number was meaningless. Yet people who saw a high number gave higher estimates than people who saw a low one. Anchors work on prices, salaries and sale tags too. What's the last anchor that fooled you?

title: Willpower Isn't a Battery (Probably)
hook_line: You've heard willpower runs out like a battery.
full_voiceover: You've heard willpower runs out like a battery. The idea is called ego depletion, and it started with a famous 1998 study. People told to eat radishes instead of nearby cookies gave up sooner on an impossible puzzle afterward. Hundreds of follow-up studies seemed to agree, and the battery idea spread into self-help books and productivity advice. Then labs tried something stricter. In 2016, one project ran a standard version in over twenty labs at once. The result? An effect close to zero. A later multi-lab project also found, at most, a very small effect. Feeling tired is real. What didn't hold up is the simple fuel-tank story, and giving up likely has many causes. Do you think willpower runs out? Tell me in the comments.
